topic.subject: science
topic.title: Nutrition in animals
topic.scope: human digestive system, digestion in mouth, stomach and intestines, absorption, villi, digestion in ruminants, amoeba

misconceptions.statement: Digestion only happens in the stomach.
misconceptions.why: The stomach is the most famous organ associated with food and hunger in everyday talk.
misconceptions.fix: Digestion begins in the mouth with saliva and continues in the small intestine where it is actually completed.

probe.question: Where does the chemical breakdown of food first begin?

misconceptions.root_belief: one organ does all the work

misconceptions.statement: Saliva only makes food slippery so it can be swallowed easily.
misconceptions.why: Students only feel the physical lubrication of saliva and cannot see the chemical breakdown of starch.
misconceptions.fix: Saliva contains enzymes that chemically break down complex starch into simpler sugars.

probe.question: If you chew bread for a long time, it tastes sweet. Why?
probe.wrong_answer: Because saliva is naturally a sweet liquid

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Stomach acid is used to melt all the food we eat into a liquid.
misconceptions.why: Students equate 'acid' with 'corrosive liquid' that dissolves everything like in cartoons.
misconceptions.fix: Stomach acid primarily kills bacteria and creates an acidic environment for protein-digesting juices to work.

probe.question: What is the main purpose of hydrochloric acid in the stomach?
probe.wrong_answer: To melt the food into a liquid state

misconceptions.statement: The large intestine is where the most important nutrients are absorbed.
misconceptions.why: Students assume the 'large' intestine is more important or that absorption happens at the very end of the journey.
misconceptions.fix: Almost all nutrient absorption happens in the small intestine; the large intestine only absorbs water and some salts.

probe.question: In which part of the digestive tract are nutrients like proteins and fats absorbed?

misconceptions.statement: Villi are tiny hairs that filter out waste from the food.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the appearance of villi with eyelashes or air filters that 'trap' things.
misconceptions.fix: Villi are finger-like outgrowths that increase surface area to help absorb digested food into the blood.

probe.question: What is the function of the villi in the small intestine?
probe.wrong_answer: To filter out dirt and waste from food

misconceptions.root_belief: biological structures act like macroscopic tools

misconceptions.statement: Humans could digest grass if we just chewed it as much as cows do.
misconceptions.why: Students think the difference is mechanical (chewing) rather than chemical (enzymes/bacteria).
misconceptions.fix: Humans lack the specific bacteria and stomach chambers required to break down cellulose found in grass.

probe.question: Why can't humans survive by eating only grass?
probe.wrong_answer: Because our teeth are not strong enough to chew it

misconceptions.root_belief: physical effort can overcome chemical limitations

misconceptions.statement: Amoeba has a tiny mouth that is too small to see.
misconceptions.why: Students believe all living things must have the same basic organs as humans (anthropomorphism).
misconceptions.fix: Amoeba has no fixed mouth; it uses temporary finger-like extensions called pseudopodia to engulf food.

probe.question: How does an Amoeba take in its food?

misconceptions.root_belief: all life must have human-like structures

misconceptions.statement: Bile is produced by the stomach to digest all types of food.
misconceptions.why: Students associate all digestive juices with the stomach and don't distinguish between food types.
misconceptions.fix: Bile is produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder; it specifically helps in the digestion of fats.

probe.question: Which organ produces bile and what does it help digest?

misconceptions.root_belief: all digestive fluids are the same

misconceptions.statement: Egestion and excretion are just two words for the same process.
misconceptions.why: Both involve removing waste from the body, and students don't distinguish between undigested food and cellular waste.
misconceptions.fix: Egestion is the removal of undigested food (faeces), while excretion is the removal of metabolic wastes like urine.

probe.question: Is the removal of undigested food called excretion?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is waste leaving the body

misconceptions.statement: Food is converted into energy inside the stomach.
misconceptions.why: Students feel an immediate 'energy boost' after eating and link it to the first place food goes.
misconceptions.fix: Food is broken down into nutrients, absorbed into the blood, and then used by cells throughout the body to release energy.

probe.question: Where is the energy from food actually released for the body to use?

misconceptions.root_belief: the start of a process is where the result happens

misconceptions.statement: Milk teeth have no roots and that is why they fall out.
misconceptions.why: Because they fall out easily, children assume they aren't 'anchored' like permanent teeth.
misconceptions.fix: Milk teeth do have roots; these roots are gradually dissolved by the permanent teeth growing underneath them.

probe.question: Why do milk teeth fall out?
probe.wrong_answer: Because they are just sitting on the gums without roots

misconceptions.root_belief: temporary things have no functional depth

misconceptions.why: The term 'four-chambered stomach' is often misinterpreted as four independent organs.
misconceptions.fix: Ruminants have a single stomach divided into four distinct compartments or chambers.

probe.question: How many stomachs does a cow have?

misconceptions.root_belief: chambers are the same as whole organs
